cards.q: Write `int firstTrue(int n, function<bool(int)> pred)`, where `pred` is false then true over `[0, n)`. Return the first index where `pred` is true, or `n` if none.
cards.a: Invariant: every index below `lo` is false and every index at or above `hi` is true. A true `mid` sets `hi = mid`, a false one sets `lo = mid + 1`, and `lo == hi` at the end is the answer.

cards.q: Write `int lowerBound(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return the first index with `a[i] >= target`, or `a.size()` if none.
cards.a: The predicate is `a[mid] >= target`, never `==`. The result can be `n`, so check `lo < n` before reading `a[lo]`.

cards.q: Write `int upperBound(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return the first index with `a[i] > target`, or `a.size()` if none.
cards.a: Only the predicate changes from lower bound: `>` instead of `>=`. `upperBound - lowerBound` is the number of copies of `target`.

cards.q: This binary search hangs on some inputs. Which condition is wrong, and why?
cards.a: `while (lo <= hi)`. When `lo == hi` and `pred(mid)` is true, `hi = mid` changes nothing and the loop never ends. The half-open form stops at `lo == hi`, so it needs `lo < hi`.

cards.q: Write `bool fits(const vector<int>& w, int k, int cap)` and `int minCapacity(const vector<int>& w, int k)` for non-empty `w`, `k >= 1`, and a total below `INT_MAX`. Return the smallest `cap` that splits `w`, in order, into at most `k` contiguous groups with each sum `<= cap`.
cards.a: `lo` starts at the largest item, because a smaller `cap` cannot hold it. `hi` is one past the largest candidate, the total, because the range is half-open.

cards.q: Write `int intSqrt(int x)` for `x >= 0`. Return the largest `r` with `r * r <= x`.
cards.a: To find the last true, search for the first false and return `lo - 1`. Use `long long`, because `mid * mid` overflows `int`.

cards.q: Write `int findMinIndex(const vector<int>& a)` for a non-empty sorted array of distinct values, rotated by any amount. Return the index of the minimum.
cards.a: Compare with the last element, not the first: `a[i] <= a[n - 1]` is false on the left part and true from the minimum onward. It also holds with no rotation at all.

cards.q: Write `int searchRotated(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for a sorted array of distinct values, rotated by any amount. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if absent.
cards.a: `pred(i)` means position `i` is at or after `target`, which makes the rotated array monotonic again. Values on the same side of the rotation compare directly; otherwise the side alone decides.

cards.q: Write `pair<int, int> twoSumSorted(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return indices `{l, r}` with `l < r` and `a[l] + a[r] == target`, or `{-1, -1}` if none.
cards.a: A sum that is too small can only grow by moving `l` up, and one that is too large can only shrink by moving `r` down. Each step discards a value that cannot be part of any answer.

cards.q: Write `int removeDuplicates(vector<int>& a)` for sorted `a`. Compact the distinct values to the front in place and return how many there are.
cards.a: Invariant: `a[0..k)` holds the distinct values seen so far. The next value is kept only if it differs from `a[k - 1]`.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> threeSum(vector<int> a)`. Return every distinct triple of values that sums to 0, each listed once.
cards.a: Skip repeats in two places: `i` against `a[i - 1]`, and `l` after a hit. `r` needs no skip, because the larger `a[l]` makes the old `a[r]` overshoot and `r` then moves on its own.

cards.q: Write `int maxWindowSum(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `1 <= k <= a.size()`. Return the maximum sum over all contiguous windows of exactly `k` elements.
cards.a: Add `a[r]`, drop `a[r - k]` once `r >= k`, and record once `r >= k - 1`. That order keeps the recorded window at exactly `k` elements.

cards.q: Write `int longestUnique(const string& s)`. Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated character.
cards.a: Grow `r` every step, then shrink `l` until the window is valid again. Record after the shrink, when `[l, r]` is valid.

cards.q: Write `int minLenAtLeast(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for positive values and positive `target`. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray with sum `>= target`, or 0 if none.
cards.a: For a shortest window, record inside the `while`, shrinking for as long as the window stays valid. Positive values are what make the sum grow and shrink with the window.

cards.q: Write `long long countAtMost(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `k >= 0`. Return how many contiguous subarrays have at most `k` distinct values.
cards.a: A valid window `[l, r]` gives `r - l + 1` subarrays ending at `r`, so add that every step. For exactly `k` distinct, use `countAtMost(a, k) - countAtMost(a, k - 1)`.

cards.q: Write `int countSumK(const vector<int>& a, int k)`, where `a` may hold negatives. Return how many contiguous subarrays sum to `k`.
cards.a: Seed `cnt[0] = 1` for subarrays that start at index 0. Query `sum - k` before adding `sum`, or `k == 0` counts an empty subarray.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> rangeAdd(int n, const vector<array<int, 3>>& ops)`, where each op `{l, r, x}` adds `x` to indices `l` through `r` of an all-zero array of size `n`. Return the final array.
cards.a: `diff` needs size `n + 1` so that `r + 1` stays in bounds. Each op is O(1), and one running sum at the end rebuilds the array.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> nextGreater(const vector<int>& a)`. For each index, return the index of the next strictly greater element to its right, or -1 if none.
cards.a: The stack holds indices still waiting for an answer, with non-increasing values. Store indices, not values, because you must write `ans[st.top()]`.

cards.q: Write `int largestRectangle(vector<int> h)` for non-negative bar heights. Return the largest rectangle area inside the histogram.
cards.a: The sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack. After a pop, the new top is the nearest smaller bar on the left, so the width is `i - l - 1`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> windowMax(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `1 <= k <= a.size()`. Return the maximum of each contiguous window of size `k`, left to right.
cards.a: The deque holds indices with strictly decreasing values, so the front is the window maximum. Evict smaller values from the back, and evict the front once `dq.front() <= i - k`.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head)`. Reverse the list iteratively and return the new head.
cards.a: Save `cur->next` before overwriting it. When the loop ends `cur` is null, so the new head is `prev`.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `ListNode* middleNode(ListNode* head)`. Return the middle node, or the second of the two middles when the length is even.
cards.a: Loop on `fast && fast->next`, testing `fast` first. `fast` moves twice as far, so `slow` is at the middle when `fast` runs out.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`, constructor `ListNode(int x)`), write `ListNode* mergeLists(ListNode* a, ListNode* b)`. Merge two sorted lists by relinking nodes and return the merged head.
cards.a: The dummy node removes the special case for the first append, so return `dummy.next`. When one list ends, one link attaches the rest of the other.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `bool hasCycle(ListNode* head)`. Return whether the list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra space.
cards.a: Compare after moving, because both pointers start equal at `head`. Inside a cycle `fast` gains one step per round, so the two must meet.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`, constructor `ListNode(int x)`), write `ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(ListNode* head, int k)`. Unlink the `k`-th node from the end, for valid `k`, and return the head.
cards.a: The dummy covers the case where the head itself is removed. Start both pointers at the dummy, `k` apart, so `slow` stops just before the target.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void preorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in node, left, right order.
cards.a: `out` must be a reference, or every call appends to its own copy.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void inorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in left, node, right order.
cards.a: On a BST this order gives the values sorted, which is the fact most problems use.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void postorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in left, right, node order.
cards.a: Children finish before the parent, which is why subtree answers such as height are computed in this order.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `vector<int> inorderIter(TreeNode* root)`. Return the in-order values using an explicit stack.
cards.a: Loop while `cur || !st.empty()`. Push the whole left spine, pop and visit one node, then move to its right child.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `int height(TreeNode* node, int& best)` and `int diameter(TreeNode* root)`. Return the largest number of edges on any path between two nodes.
cards.a: The recursion returns one thing and records another: it returns the height, a single branch, while `best` tracks the path through both branches.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root)`. Return the values grouped by depth, top to bottom and left to right.
cards.a: Save `q.size()` in `sz` before the inner loop, because the children pushed during the loop change the size.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `bool validate(TreeNode* node, long long lo, long long hi)` and `bool isValidBST(TreeNode* root)`. Return whether the tree is a strict BST, with every value inside the open range `(lo, hi)`.
cards.a: Comparing a node only with its children is the classic bug, because a whole subtree must respect every ancestor. The bounds are `long long` so that node values of `INT_MIN` and `INT_MAX` still pass.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`, constructor `TreeNode(int x)`), write `TreeNode* insertBST(TreeNode* root, int x)`. Insert `x`, which is not yet in the tree, and return the root.
cards.a: Assign the recursive result back to `root->left` or `root->right`, because that is what links the new leaf. Return `root` at every level.

cards.q: Define `struct TrieNode` with `TrieNode* next[26]` and `bool isEnd`, both default-initialised, then write `void insert(TrieNode* root, const string& word)` for lowercase words.
cards.a: `= {}` zeroes the child pointers, and without it they hold garbage. Set `isEnd` on the last node after the loop, not on the root.

cards.q: With `TrieNode` (`next[26]`, `isEnd`), write `bool search(TrieNode* root, const string& word)` for lowercase words. Return whether `word` was inserted as a whole word.
cards.a: Return `cur->isEnd`, not `true`, or any stored prefix counts as a word. A prefix check is the same loop ending in `return true`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> topK(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `k >= 1`. Return the `k` largest values in ascending order, in O(n log k) with a heap.
cards.a: Use a min-heap capped at size `k`. Its root is the smallest of the best `k`, so it is the one to evict.

cards.q: Write `struct MedianFinder` with `priority_queue<int> lo`, a min-heap `hi`, `void add(int x)` and `double median()`. `lo` holds the smaller half plus any odd element, and `median` is only called after an `add`.
cards.a: Every `x` passes through `lo` and then `hi`, which keeps all of `lo` at or below all of `hi`. Then rebalance so `lo` is never the smaller heap.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> mergeK(const vector<vector<int>>& lists)` for sorted lists, using a min-heap of `{value, list index, element index}` tuples. Return all values in sorted order.
cards.a: The heap holds at most one entry per list, so each step costs O(log k). Skip empty lists when seeding.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(vector<string>& grid, int r, int c)` and `int countIslands(vector<string>& grid)` for a non-empty grid of `'1'` land and `'0'` water. Return the number of 4-connected land regions.
cards.a: Test bounds before reading the cell, at the top of `dfs`. Overwrite `'1'` with `'0'` before recursing, or the recursion never ends.

cards.q: Write `int shortestPath(const vector<string>& grid, int sr, int sc, int tr, int tc)` with `'#'` as walls and a non-wall start. Return the fewest 4-directional steps from `(sr, sc)` to `(tr, tc)`, or -1 if unreachable.
cards.a: Set `dist` when a cell is pushed, not when it is popped, or the same cell enters the queue many times. A `dist` of -1 doubles as the unvisited mark.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> nearestSource(const vector<vector<int>>& grid)`, where cells equal to 1 are sources. Return each cell's 4-directional step distance to its nearest source, or all -1 if the grid has none.
cards.a: Push every source at distance 0 before the loop. The queue then expands all sources in lockstep, so the first visit to a cell is the shortest.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> buildGraph(int n, const vector<pair<int, int>>& edges)` for an undirected graph on nodes `0` to `n - 1`. Return the adjacency list.
cards.a: Undirected means two pushes per edge; a directed graph has only `adj[u].push_back(v)`. Size `adj` with `n` so isolated nodes still get an empty list.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> topoSort(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` for a directed graph, using Kahn's algorithm. Return a topological order, or an empty vector if the graph has a cycle.
cards.a: A node enters the queue exactly when its in-degree reaches 0. Nodes on a cycle never reach 0, so `order` ends up shorter than `n`.

cards.q: Write `bool dfs(int u, const vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& color)` and `bool hasCycle(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` with colours 0 unvisited, 1 on the current path, 2 finished. Return whether the directed graph has a cycle.
cards.a: Reaching a colour 1 node is a back edge, which means a cycle. Colour 2 nodes are finished and safe to skip, a distinction a plain `visited` flag cannot make.

cards.q: Write `struct DSU` with `vector<int> parent, sz`, a constructor `DSU(int n)`, `int find(int x)` and `bool unite(int a, int b)`. `find` compresses paths, and `unite` joins by size and returns false if `a` and `b` were already together.
cards.a: Link roots, never the original `a` and `b`, so reassign both with `find` first. Hang the smaller root under the larger and add its size.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> dijkstra(int n, const vector<vector<pair<int, int>>>& adj, int src)`, where `adj[u]` holds `{v, w}` with `w >= 0`. Return the shortest distance from `src` to every node, with `INT_MAX` for unreachable nodes.
cards.a: Skip stale entries with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;`, because a node can sit in the heap several times. Heap entries are `{dist, node}`, so that pairs order by distance.

cards.q: Write `int bellmanFord(int n, const vector<array<int, 3>>& edges, int src, int dst, int k)`, where each edge is `{u, v, w}`. Return the cheapest cost from `src` to `dst` using at most `k` edges, or `INT_MAX` if there is no such path.
cards.a: Relax from a copy of the previous round, so that each round adds at most one edge. Skip `prev[u] == INT_MAX`, or `prev[u] + w` overflows.

cards.q: Using `DSU` with `unite`, write `int kruskal(int n, vector<array<int, 3>> edges)`, where each edge is `{w, u, v}`. Return the weight of a minimum spanning tree, or -1 if the graph is disconnected.
cards.a: Putting `w` first lets a plain `sort` order the edges by weight. `unite` returning false means the edge would close a cycle, so it is skipped.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> subsets(const vector<int>& a)` for distinct values. Return all subsets.
cards.a: Record `cur` on entry, because every node of the recursion tree is a subset. Looping from `start` stops an element being reused or reordered.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, vector<bool>& used, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> permutations(const vector<int>& a)` for distinct values. Return all permutations.
cards.a: The loop restarts at 0 on every call, so `used` is what prevents repeats. Undo both `cur.push_back` and `used[i] = true` after the recursive call.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(int n, int k, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> combinations(int n, int k)`. Return all `k`-element subsets of `1` to `n`.
cards.a: Recurse with `x + 1`, so each choice only looks forward. That produces every combination exactly once, in increasing order.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, int start, int remain, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> combinationSum(vector<int> a, int target)` for positive values with possible duplicates. Return each distinct combination that sums to `target`, using each element at most once.
cards.a: Sort first, then skip with `i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]`: equal values may not open two branches at the same depth. Writing `i > 0` is the bug, because it also forbids equal values along one path.

cards.q: Write `int maxNonAdjacent(const vector<int>& a)` for non-negative values. Return the largest sum of elements with no two adjacent, in O(1) extra space.
cards.a: `prev1` is the best answer up to the previous element and `prev2` up to the one before it. Each element is either skipped (`prev1`) or taken (`prev2 + x`).

cards.q: Write `int minPathSum(const vector<vector<int>>& grid)` for a non-empty grid of non-negative values, moving only right or down. Return the smallest path sum from top-left to bottom-right, using a table with one extra row and column.
cards.a: Border cells stay `INT_MAX` so `min` ignores them, and `dp[0][1] = 0` seeds the start. The padding shifts indices, so `dp[i][j]` reads `grid[i - 1][j - 1]`.

cards.q: Write `int lengthOfLIS(const vector<int>& a)` in O(n log n) with patience sorting. Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
cards.a: `tails[i]` is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length `i + 1`. Only its size is meaningful, because `tails` itself need not be a real subsequence. `lower_bound` gives strictly increasing.

cards.q: Write `int lcs(const string& s, const string& t)`. Return the length of the longest common subsequence.
cards.a: `dp[i][j]` covers the first `i` chars of `s` and the first `j` of `t`, so the chars compared are `s[i - 1]` and `t[j - 1]`. Row 0 and column 0 stay zero for empty prefixes.

cards.q: Write `int editDistance(const string& s, const string& t)`. Return the fewest single-character inserts, deletes and replacements that turn `s` into `t`.
cards.a: Unlike LCS the borders are not zero: a prefix of length `i` needs `i` edits to match an empty string. Matching chars copy the diagonal at no cost.

cards.q: Write `int knapsack(const vector<int>& w, const vector<int>& v, int cap)` with a 1D `dp`, for items of weight `w[i]` and value `v[i]`. Return the best total value within capacity `cap`, using each item at most once.
cards.a: Loop the capacity downward, so `dp[c - w[i]]` still excludes item `i`. An upward loop lets the same item be taken twice.

cards.q: Write `int unboundedKnapsack(const vector<int>& w, const vector<int>& v, int cap)` with a 1D `dp`, for positive weights. Return the best total value within capacity `cap`, where each item may be used any number of times.
cards.a: Identical to the 0/1 form except that the capacity loop runs upward. `dp[c - w[i]]` may already include item `i`, which is exactly what allows repeats.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> mergeIntervals(vector<vector<int>> intervals)`, where each interval is `{start, end}`. Return the union as disjoint intervals sorted by start, joining intervals that touch.
cards.a: After sorting, only the last merged interval can overlap the next one. Take `max` for the new end, because the next interval may sit entirely inside the last.

cards.q: Write `int minMergeCost(const vector<int>& a)` for a non-empty row of piles, where merging two adjacent piles costs their combined size. Return the smallest total cost to merge everything into one pile.
cards.a: Loop on `len` first, so every shorter interval is ready. `k` splits `[i, j]` into `[i, k]` and `[k + 1, j]`, and the last merge always costs the sum of `[i, j]`.

cards.q: Write `int minAssignment(const vector<vector<int>>& cost)` for `n` workers and `n` jobs, where `cost[i][j]` is worker `i` doing job `j`. Return the smallest total cost, using a DP over the set of taken jobs.
cards.a: `mask` is the set of taken jobs, so the next worker is `__builtin_popcount(mask)`. Adding a bit makes the number larger, so looping masks upward finishes every subset first.

cards.q: Write `int dfs(int u, const vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& memo)` and `int longestPath(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` for a DAG, with -1 meaning not computed. Return the largest number of edges on any path.
cards.a: Read the memo on the first line and write it just before returning. `memo` must be a reference, or nothing is remembered and the run turns exponential. Use -1 as the sentinel, because 0 is a valid answer here.

cards.q: Write `int partition(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`, with `a[hi - 1]` as the pivot. Move smaller values left of the pivot and return its final index.
cards.a: `i` is the boundary: everything in `[lo, i)` is smaller than the pivot. The pivot waits at `hi - 1` during the scan and swaps into `i` at the end.

cards.q: Using `partition(a, lo, hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`, write `int quickselect(vector<int> a, int k)`. For distinct values, return the `k`-th smallest, 0-indexed, or -1 if `k` is out of range, in expected O(n).
cards.a: After `partition`, `a[p]` is in its final place, so only the side holding `k` remains. The random pivot is what avoids O(n^2) on sorted input.

cards.q: Write `void mergeSort(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`. Sort it stably, merging through a temporary vector.
cards.a: The base case is `hi - lo <= 1`, and the right half starts at `mid`, not `mid + 1`. Take from the left on `<=` to stay stable.

cards.q: Write `struct LRUCache` with `list<pair<int, int>> items` (most recent first), a map `pos` from key to list iterator, `LRUCache(int capacity)` for `capacity >= 1`, `int get(int key)` and `void put(int key, int value)`. `get` returns -1 for a missing key, and both run in O(1).
cards.a: `splice` moves a node without invalidating any iterator, so `pos` stays correct. On eviction, erase the key from `pos` before popping the list back.

cards.q: Write `long long power(long long base, long long exp, long long mod)` for `base >= 0`, `exp >= 0` and `1 < mod < 2^31`. Return `base^exp % mod` in O(log exp).
cards.a: Square `base` every step, and multiply it into `ans` only when the low bit of `exp` is set. Keeping `mod` below `2^31` keeps every product inside `long long`.

cards.q: Write `int gcd(int a, int b)` for non-negative inputs, using Euclid's algorithm. Return the greatest common divisor.
cards.a: `gcd(a, b)` equals `gcd(b, a % b)`, and the recursion stops at `b == 0` with the answer in `a`. C++17 also offers `gcd` in `<numeric>`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> sieve(int n)` for `n >= 1`, using the sieve of Eratosthenes. Return all primes up to and including `n`.
cards.a: Start crossing off at `i * i`, because smaller multiples already have a smaller prime factor. Compute that start as `1LL * i * i`, or it overflows.

cards.q: Write `struct SegTree` with `int n`, `vector<int> t` of size `2 * n`, a constructor from `const vector<int>& a`, `void update(int i, int val)` and `int query(int l, int r)`. It is a bottom-up sum tree where `query` sums the half-open range `[l, r)`.
cards.a: Leaves live at `t[n + i]`, and the parent of `i` is `i / 2`. In `query`, an odd `l` takes `t[l++]` and an odd `r` takes `t[--r]` before both climb.

cards.q: Write `struct Fenwick` with `vector<int> t`, a constructor `Fenwick(int n)`, `void add(int i, int delta)` for a 0-based `i`, and `int prefix(int i)`. `prefix` returns the sum of the first `i` elements.
cards.a: The tree is 1-based inside, so `add` starts with `i++` and `t[0]` stays unused. `i & -i` is the lowest set bit: `add` climbs by it and `prefix` strips it. The sum of `[l, r)` is `prefix(r) - prefix(l)`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> prefixFunction(const string& s)`. Return `pi`, where `pi[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `s[0..i]` that is also its suffix.
cards.a: On a mismatch fall back with `k = pi[k - 1]`, never straight to 0. To find `pat` in `text`, run this on `pat + '#' + text` and look for a value equal to `pat.size()`.

cards.q: With file-level `const long long BASE = 131, MOD = 1000000007;`, write `struct StringHash` with `vector<long long> h, p`, a constructor from `const string& s`, and `long long get(int l, int r)`. `get` returns the polynomial hash of the half-open range `[l, r)`.
cards.a: `get` subtracts the prefix shifted by `r - l` places, and the result can be negative, so add `MOD` before the last `% MOD`. Equal hashes only suggest equal strings, so confirm a match when a collision would matter.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> reservoirSample(const vector<int>& stream, int k)` for `k <= stream.size()`, using `rand()`. Return `k` elements chosen uniformly at random, in one pass and O(k) extra space.
cards.a: Element `i`, 0-based, enters with probability `k / (i + 1)` and replaces a random slot. Every element then ends up in the sample with the same chance, `k / n`.
